newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian landslide survivor "a tough bloke".
newsitem.headline: Australian landslide survivor "a tough bloke".

text.p: Stuart Diver turned his back on the stress and strain of city life several years ago to move to the tiny Australian mountain village of Thredbo to indulge his twin passions -- skiing and bushwalking.

The fit, outgoing ski instructor and hiking guide -- the sole survivor so far of a landslide that buried 20 people -- and his wife Sally are well known and liked in the close-knit Snowy Mountains town, which has a permanent population of 500.

Sally Diver, a receptionist at a village hotel, was still missing as night fell on Saturday, buried somewhere in the tonnes of rubble, mud and rock that mark the site of a landslide that wrecked two ski lodges on Wednesday night.
"He is a tough bloke," fellow Thredbo resident Ryan Taylor said of his 27-year-old friend. "He is definitely ... one of the guys who would survive this."
Fire Brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer told reporters it was that toughness and Diver's training on the ski fields which had probably kept him alive.
"He's a trained expert in search and rescue here on the snowfields," Krimmer said.
"It's probably his own training and mental fortitude which have brought him through this."
Friends described Diver as a bit of a fitness fanatic.
"Stuart was very handsome, extremely fit of course and was devoted to helping and caring for others," said a close friend.

Like many men in small Australian bush towns, Diver joined the local volunteer fire brigade along with his brother, Ewan, who is among the 500 rescuers involved in the grim and dangerous task of searching for survivors.
Diver, originally from Melbourne, Australia's second biggest city, has a reputation for determination and for throwing himself passionately into everything he does.
As a ski instructor, Diver is one of the most qualified on the Thredbo slopes.
"He is dedicated to his profession, it is his passion," said a fellow instructor. "You don't get to where he is without a lot of hard work."

Australia's ski season is brief, June to October, and Diver spent his summers guiding tourists through the national park surrounding the country's highest mountain, the 2,230 metre (6,700 feet) Mount Kosciuszko.
"I was impressed by his willingness to get out there and learn about the summer side of the operation ... animals and flora," said a friend of the Divers, Ian Talbot.
Steve Hodge, who drives the local Thredbo bus and would give the ski instructors a lift to the ski lifts, described Diver as easy-going and well-liked in the small Thredbo community.
"He's young and he's fit. He's a very well-liked man. He's just a top bloke," he said.
Hodge said Diver's feat of survival had inspired the community, which had begun to despair of finding someone alive.
"It's pretty solemn but we are all banding together. There's a big hype now and we're all going, 'come on get him out'".

Diver is well known around Thredbo, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney. Both he and his wife, about 30, would work out at the Thredbo Alpine Training Centre, which is part of the Australian government's Australian Institute of Sport.
A recent fitness test showed he was capable of being an elite athlete, a worker at the centre told Reuters.
"He would often come in with Sally and train together," the woman said. "He is probably one of the fittest people in here."
The woman said of Sally: "She's a lovely lady and everyone loves her as much as they love him. We love them both."
